name: Bilberry extract

card.summary: Anthocyanin-rich European blueberry extract with a folk reputation for vision; trials are small and no cosmetic eye-brightening evidence exists.
card.aka: Vaccinium myrtillus, European blueberry, whortleberry, blaeberry
card.note: Reputation for eyes rests on folklore and anecdote; no published trial tests it for brightening eyes.

quick.overview:
Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) is a dark-berried shrub of northern Europe, related to the blueberry. Its fruit and standardised extracts are sold as supplements, traditionally for eye complaints.
In appearance circles it is sometimes mentioned for brighter eyes. Registered trials of bilberry cover dry eye, blood sugar, lipids, cognition and heart disease, and none listed targets cosmetic eye appearance.
quick.mechanism: The berries are rich in anthocyanins, pigments with antioxidant properties in laboratory studies. Proposed mechanisms for eye or vascular effects are largely extrapolated from lab and animal work.
quick.risks: Whole berries are a common food. Encyclopedic sources report no proven health benefit from eating them and note that a review of low-quality studies found no evidence of improved night vision.

lead: Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) is a low-growing shrub native to northern Europe, with dark blue-black berries that are eaten fresh and processed into jams, liqueurs and dried powders or standardised extracts sold as dietary supplements [1][2]. The berries are rich in anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their colour, along with other polyphenols and tannins [2].

For appearance, bilberry is used in two ways. Supplement marketing and folk tradition connect it to eye health and, by extension, clearer, brighter-looking eyes; and a 2024 randomised trial tested a fermented bilberry extract for crow's feet wrinkles, skin firmness and skin tone, reporting improvements in wrinkle depth, elasticity and complexion over 84 days [16]. The anthocyanin-antioxidant rationale is the common thread: proponents say these pigments protect tissue from oxidative stress and inflammation, which research reviews have examined in cell, animal and clinical studies [13][17].

Bilberry has a folk reputation for helping the eyes. A frequently repeated anecdote describes British pilots in World War II attributing better night vision to bilberry jam, reported in a secondary source as an anecdote [1]. Encyclopedic sources note that a review of low-quality clinical studies did not find improved night vision [2]. Registered studies concern dry eye, glycaemic response, lipids, cognition and cardiovascular recovery [3][4].

paras: Bilberry is a perennial shrub of heaths and coniferous forests across northern Europe, with some range in northern Asia and North America. It is distinct from, though related to, cultivated blueberries and cranberries [1]. Regional names include whortleberry in southern England, blaeberry in Scotland and northern England, and fraochán in Ireland; the name appears to be Scandinavian in origin [1][2]. Unlike North American blueberries, bilberries are dark inside, grow singly or in pairs and have a smooth, round end opposite the stalk [2].

Bilberries grow in acidic, nutrient-poor soils and are rarely cultivated because the plant is hard to grow and the fruit small, so most come from wild harvests in northern and central Europe [2]. Sweden, Iceland and Ireland have harvesting traditions, including Ireland's Bilberry Sunday [2]. The berries are eaten fresh or made into jams, juices, pies and liqueurs, and their pigment stains the lips, fingers and tongue [2].
Reported anthocyanin content is high, and laboratory analyses of berries describe anthocyanins as the main phenolic constituents of bilberry; their content can exceed that of blueberries [2][5].

A 2024 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested a fermented bilberry extract in 66 people with visible crow's feet, mild-to-moderate skin slackness and uneven skin tone. Wrinkle depth, smoothness, firmness, elasticity, skin colour and antioxidant capacity were measured at 28, 56 and 84 days alongside dermatologist evaluation and self-assessment. At day 84 wrinkle depth had decreased by 10.6 percent, firmness had improved by 13.3 percent and elasticity by 12.4 percent, skin antioxidant capacity rose 20.8 percent, and a measure of skin lightness and redness shifted toward a brighter, less red complexion, with statistically significant differences from placebo [16].

Supplement sellers also link bilberry to eye comfort and eye brightness. A 12-week randomised, double-blind trial of bilberry extract reported improved objective measures of ciliary muscle contraction in the eye, relevant to eye strain [18].

Traditional medicine uses bilberry, and supplements are marketed mainly for eye disorders [2]. The World War II pilot anecdote remains widely repeated [1]. A Spanish ophthalmology journal article reviewed Vaccinium myrtillus in eye medicine [19], and a diabetic rat study reported that an extract delayed blood-retinal barrier breakdown [20].

Grokipedia traces the English word bilberry to a Danish-origin term, with the Oxford English Dictionary's earliest citation in 1584 in the writings of John Dee, a description in Gerard's Herball in 1597, and Linnaeus's formal naming of Vaccinium myrtillus in 1753; Wikipedia gives a similar but slightly different etymological dating, placing the name's likely Scandinavian roots as early as 1577.[1][2]

Traditional European medicine used the fruit and leaves for a range of complaints. Grokipedia reports that Dioscorides recommended the fruit for diarrhoea, that sixteenth-century writers listed urinary, scurvy and biliary uses, and that leaf teas were used for diabetes in parts of Europe and Russia.[1] McGill University's Office for Science and Society likewise notes folk uses for circulatory problems, diarrhoea and ulcers.[27]

In Ireland the berries were traditionally gathered on Bilberry Sunday, the last Sunday of July, linked to the Lughnasadh harvest festival, and in Sweden bilberries grow across roughly a sixth of the land area according to Wikipedia.[2]

The best-known bilberry story holds that British pilots in World War II ate bilberry jam and gained sharper night vision, which helped them in night combat.[1][27] Joe Schwarcz of McGill's Office for Science and Society writes that no documented evidence shows the pilots ate it, and notes accounts suggesting the story was circulated to draw attention away from British airborne radar; some versions credit carrots instead.[27]

Later human work tested the idea directly. Research groups at the Naval Aerospace Research Laboratory in Florida and at Tel Aviv University gave young men a placebo or an extract providing up to 40 mg of anthocyanins and then measured night visual acuity; both reported no improvement.[27][28] Wikipedia cites a 2004 review of low-quality studies reaching the same conclusion for night vision.[2] The same sources note laboratory findings that a blueberry anthocyanin extract protected retinal cells from hydrogen peroxide in culture, and that no clinical trials have tested anthocyanin supplements for macular degeneration.[27][28]

Bilberry appears in appearance discussion in two ways. One is the eye angle: supplement sellers and herbal tradition link it to eye comfort and eye health, and some users hope for clearer, whiter or brighter-looking eyes. The other is the skin angle, based on the 2024 fermented-bilberry trial and on the general antioxidant-anthocyanin rationale.[16][17] It is also named in general supplement threads on T Nation.[26]

Extracts are sold standardised to a stated anthocyanin percentage, which Grokipedia gives as roughly 25 to 36 percent anthocyanidins, and branded extracts such as Mirtoselect appear in registered trials.[1][12]

Review articles describe berry anthocyanins as antioxidants and discuss possible roles in cardiovascular, neurological and ocular health, but these are largely laboratory and population-level findings [13]. A 2022 review reported that cell and animal studies show bilberry lowering inflammatory signals such as TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-1 beta and altering NF-kappa B signalling, and that bilberry fruit, juice and anthocyanin supplementation lowered inflammatory markers in most clinical studies in metabolic disorders [17]. A mouse study reported that anthocyanin-rich bilberry extract improved blood sugar and insulin sensitivity through AMPK activation [14]. Cell studies have reported apoptosis in cancer cells exposed to bilberry anthocyanins [15].

The 2024 randomised trial in 66 people on skin ageing and brightness is described above [16]. A 2012 randomised trial reported that bilberries reduced low-grade inflammation in people with features of metabolic syndrome [21]. A freeze-dried bilberry supplement improved walking distance and lipids after myocardial infarction in an open-label randomised trial [22], and a related pragmatic trial reported decreased blood microvesicles [23]. A cross-over trial of isolated anthocyanins from bilberry and black rice reported no effect on LDL cholesterol or other cardiovascular biomarkers in adults with elevated cholesterol [24].

A registered trial of bilberry-containing capsules for dry eye enrolled 80 participants [3]. Other registered studies examine bilberry for myocardial infarction recovery (a phase 4 trial, n=50, and a larger trial of bilberry and oat intake, n=900) [4][6], glycaemic response (small studies, n=8 and n=32) [7][8], blood lipids with black rice anthocyanins (n=55) [9], metabolism in healthy people (n=80) [10] and cognition and mood (n=61 and n=76) [11][12]. The registry entries give designs and populations but no results.

Wikipedia states that there is no substantial clinical evidence of health benefits from the fruit or its preparations and that a review of low-quality studies found no improvement in night vision [2].

Bilberry fruit is a common food, and its pigment temporarily stains lips, fingers and tongue [2]. Supplement extracts fall under herbal product rules, and an overview of 50 systematic reviews of herbal medicine adverse effects shows how harm profiles vary widely between herbs, from minor to serious [25].

Grokipedia states that short-term use of extract at moderate amounts is generally well tolerated, with rare mild digestive upset reported, and that bilberry's possible antiplatelet effects have led to suggestions that people on anticoagulants such as warfarin discuss it with a clinician; it adds that most trials are small and short.[1]

Bilberry extract is sold in capsules, standardised extracts (a branded bilberry extract, Mirtoselect, appears in a registered cognition trial [12]) and blends, and is among the products named in T Nation supplement threads [26].

timeline.event: The Oxford English Dictionary records the first English use of the word bilberry, in writing by John Dee, as reported by Grokipedia [1].
Linnaeus formally names Vaccinium myrtillus in Species Plantarum [1].
Gerard's Herball describes the bilberry, according to Grokipedia.[1]
A review of low-quality clinical studies finds no evidence that bilberry improves night vision, as cited by Wikipedia.[2]
A double-blind trial of the Mirtoselect extract in dry eye is reported by Grokipedia to show improved tear film stability.[1]
McGill's Office for Science and Society publishes an explainer on the bilberry and night-vision claim.[27]
A randomised trial of fermented bilberry extract reports changes in wrinkle depth, elasticity and skin tone over 84 days.[16]

lore.intro: Bilberry is discussed in supplement and wellness circles mainly for eyes and, more recently, skin, and it turns up in general T Nation supplement threads.[26]

claims.claim: British pilots saw better at night after eating bilberry jam
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and popular retellings credit bilberry jam with sharpening night vision in WWII night fighters.[1]
claims.experts: Schwarcz writes that no documented evidence shows the pilots ate it, and two placebo-controlled studies in Florida and Tel Aviv found no night-vision gain from anthocyanin extracts.[27][28]

claims.believers: Proponents point to anthocyanin antioxidants and to eye supplements built on them.[13]
claims.experts: Cell studies show protection of retinal cells, while no clinical trials had tested anthocyanin supplements for macular degeneration as of the 2019 explainers; a 12-week trial reported improved ciliary muscle measures and a dry-eye trial is registered.[27][18][3]

claims.claim: Bilberry brightens skin and softens crow's feet
claims.believers: Some supplement brands cite antioxidant and anti-aging effects of anthocyanins.[17]
claims.experts: A 2024 randomised, double-blind trial in 66 people reported reduced wrinkle depth and improved elasticity and tone at day 84 versus placebo for a fermented extract.[16]

claims.claim: Anthocyanins cut inflammation and help blood sugar
claims.believers: Users cite lowered inflammatory markers and improved insulin sensitivity.[17][14]
claims.experts: A 2012 trial and a 2022 review report lowered inflammatory markers in metabolic-risk groups, a mouse study reported better glycaemia, and an isolated-anthocyanin crossover trial found no change in LDL cholesterol.[21][17][14][24]

claims.believers: Laboratory papers describing apoptosis in cancer cells are cited as support.[15]
claims.experts: The work cited is in cell culture; no trial in this record tests bilberry against cancer.[15]
